summary: Describes the resource transponder, an automatic mechanism for keeping resource location information up to date. It is an informational paper.

plainLanguage.summary: A tag on a thing that automatically tells the directory when the thing moves.

questions: how do resource transponders keep locations updated
why are resource location systems hard to maintain
subtitle: Automatic agents that keep resource directories up to date when files move.

tldr.problem: Information location systems like Gopher and WAIS contain pointers that quickly become outdated when resources are moved or modified, requiring constant manual maintenance.
tldr.mechanism: The resource transponder system attaches metadata and an intelligent agent to each resource. When the resource moves, the agent automatically notifies the directory system with updated location information.
tldr.outcome: Resource location information can stay accurate without manual updates from either the directory maintainer or the resource owner, making Internet information systems more scalable as the number of publishers grows.

today: RFC 1728 is an Informational RFC that proposes the concept of resource transponders but does not specify a protocol. It remains an idea that was not standardized or widely implemented.

sections.title: The Problem with Manual Maintenance
sections.content:
Information systems on the Internet like Archie, Gopher and WAIS help people find files and resources, but they contain pointers rather than the actual resources. When a resource is moved, modified or becomes obsolete, the pointers go stale. Currently, directories update these pointers by contacting every resource on a schedule (Archie does this every 30 days), but this means the information can be up to 30 days out of date and requires significant computing resources.

The real problem is two-sided: directory maintainers must track every change to thousands of resources, while people running resources must notify every directory where their resource appears whenever it changes. This is not scalable as more people become publishers on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move house, you have to tell the post office, and the post office has to tell everyone's address books. This gets harder as more people move around.

sections.title: Requirements for a Solution
sections.content:
Any solution must reduce the manual work needed for both indexing and pointer maintenance. It must increase the reliability and accuracy of resource location systems, because outdated information is worse than no information. The system must also provide security, allowing resource owners to control who can access their resources through the location system.

Finally, the solution must be easy enough for non-experts such as librarians and database maintainers to use, without requiring deep technical knowledge to publish their resources.
sections.plainLanguage: A good system needs to be automatic, accurate, secure and easy for non-experts to use.

sections.title: How Resource Transponders Work
sections.content:
The resource transponder system adds two layers to every resource: a metainformation layer and an agent layer. The metainformation is metadata physically attached to the resource—like a Uniform Resource Name (URN), title, URL, and size—that describes what the resource is and where it is. When the resource moves, this metadata moves with it.

The agent is a program attached to or running alongside the resource. Its job is to read the metainformation and use it to update resource location systems automatically. When a resource moves to a new location, the agent can contact its old location to determine whether copies still exist there, update the directory with the new location, and delete old pointers if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Each resource gets a name tag with its information, and a robot that can phone directories to say 'I've moved to this address.'

sections.title: How Metainformation and Agents Can Be Implemented
sections.content:
The metainformation layer can be stored in many ways depending on the type of resource. For active resources like online catalogs, it can live in a file with a well-known name. For text documents, it could be stored as the first or last bytes of the file (guaranteeing it moves with the resource) or as a companion file with a related name like 'paper.meta' alongside 'paper.txt'. Agents could be embedded in the resource file itself or run as a separate program on the computer.

Agents can also be implemented flexibly. On simple systems, one agent per computer can be activated whenever a resource arrives on that machine. In more sophisticated systems, each resource can have its own agent that runs continuously, mediating access to the resource and handling security, encryption and translation as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The robot and the name tag can be designed in different ways depending on what kind of resource you have and what kind of computer it lives on.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The resource transponder system enables important security improvements. By requiring the resource owner to explicitly publish their resource through an agent, the system can ensure that only the resource owner decides which directories get pointers to it. This prevents unauthorized public exposure of resources that should be restricted.

When agents mediate access to resources, they can handle encryption, access control and authentication. A resource owner could encrypt their data and let the agent decrypt it only for authorized users, providing protection against both directory system compromise and unauthorized network access.
sections.plainLanguage: The robot can ask for a password before letting people access the resource, and can keep the resource's location secret from directories that shouldn't know about it.

sections.title: Where This Stands Now
sections.content: RFC 1728 is an informational paper presenting one possible approach to solving the resource location and maintenance problem. It is not a protocol specification, but rather a research proposal describing the concept of resource transponders and how they might be implemented. The author notes that if there is consensus that resource transponders are potentially useful, the next step would be to design actual protocol specifications and standards for them.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is not a finished design, but an idea about how things could work. It's looking for feedback before anyone builds the actual system.
